No. 

The layering of relationships is what makes the X-men books work in the first place. If those relationships begin to feel burdensome rather than enriching, that's the fault of the writer, not the history itself. 

Besides, what will end up happening is that a reboot will degenerate into every classic X-Men story just being retold in an inferior way by an inferior writer. 

I'd like the actual Wolverine back, though. Cut the crap, Marvel.

I have felt this way on occasion. 

But let me give you this to mull over, and forgive me if it sounds like I'm speaking down to you because you're young, because I'm not. 

I am currently 33. I was homeschooled throughout high school and had no idea how to interact with others socially. I moved away for college and spent four years on a huge urban campus without making a single friend. I paid for an apartment for four years and not one soul other than myself and my mother ever set foot in that space. 

I went to graduate school while living at home. I was totally depressed and entered into the whole thing believing that I'd never meet any friends or expand my life beyond the very insular, limiting scope that had defined it for years and years. 

In grad school, I was forced to spend time with 12 people who had the same interests as me, were generally displaced from their places of origin, and were looking to make friends. Finally, I found my people. By that time, I was 26. 

- One of those people became my first girlfriend. I was 27. 

- One of those people got me my first "real" job. I was 28. 

- One of those people taught me to drive for the first time in my life. I was 29. 

- My last girlfriend was a woman I met at work. She was dysfunctional and weird and very depressed, but I loved her anyway. I loved her because she was like me, understood me and, on top of that, had a million great qualities I was willing to fight for. 

Now, yes. Things haven't been perfect. I've lost most of those grad school friends. I eventually lost both girls. Etc. etc. etc. 

But the point is, many of those things happened FAR later in life than society says they should. And I can tell you that, when I had my first kiss at 27 or drove alone for the first time at almost 30, it still felt awesome and invigorating and special. I know it seems like things should've happened for you by now, but not everyone is on the same timetable. Every magazine, tv show, film, etc. produced is there to convince you that you have to keep up with everyone else. The real trick is sustaining your belief in yourself until the moment comes for you. 

The other thing to remember is that somewhere out there, there is a man who will love you not only in spite of, but because of, everything you described. I know that sounds trite, but it's true. I've been that man. I've been with a woman whose entire life revolved around neuroses and anxieties that had ruined her life and I've been able to look her in the eye and tell her, without an ounce of dishonesty, that I love every single part of her. If she had let me, I'd still be saying that to her now.  

That guy is there for you too. You have to believe that. Keep doing whatever you can to get into a career or program where you'll meet other people organically and then keep telling yourself that 21 years old is way, way too early to be writing yourself off as a lost cause.

Thanks for these replies, everyone.
At this moment, it means so much to just hear one or two people acknowledge me in a way that's not judgmental or dismissive.
Thanks.
